title: Awake, Arm of the LORD: The Cup of Wrath Removed
summary: God calls the faithful to look back to Abraham and Sarah, from whom he made a great people out of one man, and promises to turn Zion's ruins into a garden like Eden. The people cry for the LORD's arm to wake as it did when he defeated the sea at the exodus. God answers with comfort and turns the cry around: it is Jerusalem that must wake, because he has taken from her hand the cup of his wrath and will give it to her tormentors.
story: Chapter 50 ended with a call to trust the LORD in the dark. Chapter 51 speaks to exactly those people, the ones who pursue righteousness and seek the LORD but see only ruins. The chapter reaches back to the beginning of Israel's story (Abraham and Sarah, Eden, the exodus) to say that the God who acted then has not changed. It also begins a run of urgent double commands (“Awake, awake”) that carries into chapter 52 and builds toward the announcement that God is returning to Zion, which leads straight into the fourth Servant Song.
historical:
The chapter speaks to a people who feel small and exposed. Its images fit the aftermath of Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC: sons lying faint in the streets, devastation, famine, and sword (verses 19 and 20), and a captive people who live in fear of an oppressor (verse 13). Most scholars place these words among the exiles in Babylon before Cyrus of Persia captured the city in 539 BC; those who hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book read them as prophecy of that same situation. The promise that the captive will not die in the dungeon (verse 14) gave hope to people who had seen family members deported, imprisoned, or killed.

The backward look to Abraham mattered to a community that had lost land, king, and temple. Ezekiel 33:24 records people in ruined Judah arguing that if Abraham, being only one man, possessed the land, then surely they, being many, would keep it. Isaiah 51 uses the same memory for the opposite purpose: not to boast that they deserve the land, but to trust that God can make much out of little.
cultural:
Verses 9 and 10 draw on imagery shared across the ancient Near East, where the raging sea often stood for chaos. Texts from ancient Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast whose clay tablets were discovered from 1929 onward, tell of the storm god Baal defeating Yam (Sea) and a coiling sea monster. The Old Testament borrows this language without the mythology. Rahab here is not the woman of Jericho in Joshua 2 but a name for a sea monster, and elsewhere a poetic nickname for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7; Psalm 87:4). The prophet fuses creation and exodus: the God who mastered the chaos waters is the God who dried up the Red Sea to make a road for the redeemed.

The cup of wrath (verses 17 and 22) was a well-known prophetic image. Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink the cup of God's wrath until they staggered (Jeremiah 25:15-16), and Psalm 75:8 pictures the LORD holding a foaming cup that the wicked must drain to the dregs. The picture is of drunkenness without wine: a people reeling and helpless under judgment. Verse 23 draws on the ancient practice of conquerors humiliating the defeated by treading on them; Joshua 10:24 shows Israel's commanders placing their feet on the necks of captured kings.
literary: The chapter is built around repeated calls. Three times God says “Listen to Me” or its equivalent (verses 1, 4, and 7), each followed by a promise. Then come three urgent double imperatives. The first, “Awake, awake” in verse 9, is the people's cry to the arm of the LORD; the second, in verse 17, is God's call to Jerusalem; the third opens chapter 52, calling Zion to clothe herself with strength. The effect is a dialogue: the people ask God to wake up, and God replies that he is not the one asleep. The imagery of garments and moths in verses 6 and 8 echoes 50:9, so that the Servant's enemies and Zion's oppressors share the same fate.

outline.t: Look to Abraham and Sarah: Zion's desert will become Eden
God's justice and salvation will outlast heaven and earth
The people's cry: awake, arm of the LORD, as at the Red Sea
God's answer: I am the one who comforts you
Jerusalem, wake up: the cup of wrath is taken away

doctrines.note: The call to look to Abraham and Sarah grounds hope in God's covenant promise to multiply one childless couple into a people (Genesis 12:1-3; 15:5). The God who kept that promise against impossible odds will keep it again.

“My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail” (verse 6). Salvation here is God's saving action in history, and it is more permanent than the created world itself. Heaven and earth will wear out; his rescue will not.

The cup of wrath shows that judgment is real and that Jerusalem drank it. But the chapter ends with God removing the cup and promising she will never drink it again. Judgment in Isaiah is never God's last word to his people.

words.note: Nacham, in this form to comfort or console. It appears four times in the chapter (verses 3, 12, and twice in 19), taking up the opening words of chapter 40, “Comfort, comfort My people.” In verse 12 God doubles the pronoun: “I, even I, am He who comforts you.” The comfort is not a feeling offered from a distance but God's own presence and action.

Zeroa, arm, the common Old Testament symbol of strength in action. God brought Israel out of Egypt “with an outstretched arm” (Deuteronomy 26:8). Here the arm will bring justice to the nations (verse 5) and is called to wake as in the days of old (verse 9). The same word returns in 52:10 and 53:1, where the arm of the LORD is revealed in the despised Servant.

Kos, cup. A cup in the Old Testament can stand for a person's allotted portion, whether blessing (Psalm 23:5) or judgment (Psalm 75:8). Here it is the cup of God's fury, which Jerusalem has drained. The image lies behind Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane that the cup might pass from him (Mark 14:36).

christ: The chapter's movement from Abraham to a multitude and from ruin to Eden is the shape of the whole biblical story, which the New Testament sees completed in Christ, the offspring of Abraham in whom the nations are blessed (Galatians 3:8, 16). The cup is the clearest link. In Gethsemane Jesus asked his Father to remove the cup from him if possible, yet submitted to drink it (Mark 14:36), and the church has long read that cup against passages like this one: the cup God takes from his people's hand is the cup his Son takes into his own. The chapter itself does not say how God removes the cup; it promises only that he will. The next two chapters, with their Servant who bears the sins of many, give the first answer, and the Gospels show where Christians believe it was fulfilled.
questions: Why might remembering Abraham and Sarah, one old couple with no child, be more encouraging to a discouraged community than a promise of sudden strength?
The people cry to God to wake up, and God tells Jerusalem to wake up. When have you been waiting for God when he may have been waiting for you?
Verse 12 asks why people fear mortals who wither like grass. What human powers loom largest in your fears, and what would it change to see them as this chapter does?
